results.title: Static, Quasi-Static, and Dynamic (Fatigue) Testing: Key Differences in Standards and Equipment | Frank Bacon %
results.content: # Static, Quasi-Static, and Dynamic (Fatigue) Testing: Key Differences in Standards and Equipment. When evaluating materials, components, or full assemblies, engineers rely on testing to ensure products perform reliably and meet industry standards. Depending on the application, tests may be **static**, **quasi-static**, or **dynamic (fatigue)** in nature. Each testing method serves a unique purpose and requires specialized equipment. Static testing applies a **single load** or force to a specimen and holds it until failure or deformation occurs. * ASTM E8/E8M – Tensile testing of metals. * ASTM D638 – Tensile testing of plastics. * ISO 6892 – Metallic materials tensile testing. * **Universal Testing Machines (UTMs):** Servo-hydraulic or electromechanical load frames equipped with load cells and extensometers. * **Grips and fixtures** designed for tension, compression, flexure, or shear tests. Static testing is straightforward but essential—it provides the baseline mechanical properties for design. Quasi-static testing is similar to static testing but performed at **very slow, controlled rates of loading or displacement**. It simulates conditions where materials or components experience gradual loads over time but not high-speed or repeated cycles. * ASTM D695 – Compressive properties of plastics. * ISO 604 – Plastics compression testing. * ASTM D790 – Flexural properties of plastics and composites. * **Electromechanical test frames** with precise crosshead speed control. Quasi-static tests bridge the gap between simple static strength and high-speed dynamics. Dynamic or fatigue testing subjects materials/components to **cyclic loading**—repeated stresses or strains over thousands or millions of cycles. Most failures in real-world service occur due to fatigue, not single overload events. Aerospace, automotive, medical device, and energy industries all rely heavily on fatigue testing data. * ASTM E466 – Fatigue testing of metallic materials. * ASTM D7791 – Fatigue of plastics. * ISO 1099 – Fatigue testing of metals. * ASTM E647 – Crack growth rate. * **Servo-hydraulic fatigue test systems** capable of high-frequency cyclic loading. * **Resonant fatigue machines** for efficient high-cycle testing. Dynamic testing requires high-precision control systems that can apply millions of cycles without equipment drift or failure. * **Static testing** → Single load until failure. * **Quasi-static testing** → Slow, controlled loading. * **Dynamic (fatigue) testing** → Repeated cyclic loading.
